questions.question: The chapter's epigraph argues against a particular position about two-phase commit. Who wrote it, and where?

options.text: James Corbett et al., Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database (2012)
Theo Härder and Andreas Reuter, Principles of Transaction-Oriented Database Recovery (1983)
Jim Gray, The Transaction Concept (1981)
Eric Brewer, Towards Robust Distributed Systems (2000)

questions.explanation: The position it argues against is that you should code around the absence of transactions rather than pay for them.

questions.question: Which things does the chapter list as going wrong 'in the harsh reality of data systems'? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The database software or hardware may fail at any time, including in the middle of a write operation; and the application may crash at any time, including halfway through a series of operations
Interruptions in the network can unexpectedly cut off the application from the database, or one database node from another
Several clients may write at the same time, overwriting each other's changes; and a client may read data that doesn't make sense because it has only partially been updated
Client clocks may drift apart from one another, so writes end up being applied to the database in the wrong order and later writes silently lose

questions.explanation: Clock drift belongs to Chapter 8, not to this list. The fourth item the chapter does name is that race conditions between clients can cause surprising bugs. Six things in all. Ensuring these don't cause catastrophic failure requires a lot of work — and a lot of testing.

questions.question: Give the chapter's definition of a transaction.

options.text: Grouping several reads and writes into one logical unit
A single atomic write applied to exactly one object in the database
A lock held on a set of rows for the duration of a client session
A durable log entry describing a change that has been applied

questions.explanation: No partial failure is the property that everything else in the chapter builds on.

questions.question: 'Transactions are not a law of nature.' What were they created for?

options.text: To simplify the programming model for applications using the database
To improve write throughput by batching many writes together
To enable distributed consensus between the database nodes
To satisfy the audit requirements imposed by financial regulators

questions.explanation: Programmer convenience, purchased from the database at a cost.

questions.question: Does the chapter claim every application needs transactions?

options.text: No — weakening or abandoning them can buy performance or availability
Yes — every application that writes any data at all needs them
Only applications handling financial data genuinely need them
Only applications distributed across several machines need them

questions.explanation: To decide, you need to understand exactly what safety guarantees transactions can provide and what costs are associated with them — and although transactions seem straightforward at first glance, there are many subtle but important details.

questions.question: Where does today's transaction style come from, and how much has it changed?

options.text: The style introduced in 1975 by IBM System R, the first SQL database
From Oracle in 1985, and it has been rewritten several times since
From the SQL standard in 1992, replacing earlier incompatible designs
From the ACID paper in 1983, with no earlier implementation

questions.explanation: 40 years of near-continuity is the chapter's point. Almost all relational databases today, and some nonrelational databases, support transactions.

questions.question: What were NoSQL databases aiming for in the late 2000s, and what does the chapter call the main casualty?

options.text: New data models, plus replication and partitioning by default
Stronger consistency guarantees, with durability as the main casualty
Better query languages, with secondary indexing as the casualty
Lower operating cost, with replication as the main casualty

questions.explanation: Redefining the word is the part that makes vendor claims hard to compare.

questions.question: What two opposing beliefs about transactions does the chapter dismiss, and how?

options.text: That transactions and scalability are fundamentally incompatible
It endorses the first of the two views and rejects the second outright
It endorses the second of the two views and rejects the first outright
It declines to take any position between the two competing views

questions.explanation: The truth is not that simple: like every other technical design choice, transactions have advantages and limitations, which the chapter explores both in normal operation and in various extreme but realistic circumstances.

questions.question: Expand ACID, and give its authors, year and motivation.

options.text: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — coined in 1983
Atomicity, Concurrency, Isolation, Durability — coined by Jim Gray in 1981 for transaction processing
Availability, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — coined by Codd in 1970
Atomicity, Consistency, Integrity, Durability — coined by the SQL standard committee in 1992

questions.explanation: The irony the chapter notes: the term intended to establish precision has become imprecise.

questions.question: Why has ACID 'become mostly a marketing term'?

options.text: Because one database's ACID does not equal another's, especially isolation
Because the acronym itself was trademarked and could not be reused
Because the four properties turn out to be impossible to implement together
Because the great majority of databases are not in fact ACID compliant

questions.explanation: The high-level idea is sound, but the devil is in the details.

questions.question: Expand BASE, and give the chapter's assessment.

options.text: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency
Basic Atomicity, Serializability, Eventual durability — a precise weaker standard
Balanced Availability and Strong Eventual consistency — stricter than ACID
Best Available State Estimate — a consistency model

questions.explanation: Systems that do not meet the ACID criteria are sometimes called BASE, which is defined only negatively.

questions.question: Contrast the multi-threaded-programming meaning of 'atomic' with the ACID meaning.

options.text: That no other thread can observe a half-finished operation
They mean exactly the same thing
ACID atomicity is about concurrency; the threading sense is about durability
The threading sense is about crashes; the ACID sense is about locking

questions.explanation: A trap because the word is genuinely overloaded across branches of computing.

questions.question: What does ACID atomicity actually describe, and which example faults does the chapter give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: What happens if a client wants to make several writes but a fault occurs after some of the writes have been processed — the transaction is aborted and the database must discard or undo any writes it has made so far in that transaction
The process crashes, or the network connection is interrupted
The disk becomes full, or some integrity constraint is violated
Two clients write to the same object simultaneously, and one of the two writes is silently lost

questions.explanation: The last one is isolation's territory, not atomicity's.

questions.question: Why is the absence of atomicity specifically a retry problem?

options.text: Because you wouldn't know how much of the change had taken effect
Because a retry will always fail unless the writes were atomic to begin with
Because atomicity is what prevents a transaction from being retried at all
Because a safe retry depends on durability rather than on atomicity

questions.explanation: Knowability is what makes retry safe.

questions.question: Which word does the chapter say would have been better than 'atomicity', and why does it keep 'atomicity' anyway?

options.text: Abortability — the ability to discard all of a transaction's writes
Indivisibility, except that the word is too long to be practical
Durability, except that the term is already used for something else
Isolation, except that it would confuse readers of the standard

questions.explanation: Abortability names the mechanism; atomicity names the appearance.

questions.question: Match each usage of 'consistency' to its meaning. (Select all that apply.)

options.text: In Chapter 5, replica consistency and eventual consistency in asynchronously replicated systems
In storage engines, the consistency of a B-tree index with the rows it indexes
In the CAP theorem, linearizability
In ACID, an application-specific notion of the database being in a 'good state'

questions.explanation: Index consistency is not one of the four senses listed. The fourth is consistent hashing, used in partitioning and rebalancing. It's unfortunate that the same word is used with at least four different meanings.

questions.question: Give the accounting example for ACID consistency, and say whose responsibility it is.

options.text: Invariants about your data that must always hold true
It means all replicas hold the same data, and is the database's responsibility
It means reads return the latest write, and is the client's responsibility
It means the schema is enforced, and is the administrator's responsibility

questions.explanation: Application-defined invariants are the ones the database cannot know about.

questions.question: What is the chapter's argument for evicting C from ACID?

options.text: Consistency is the application's responsibility; the other three are the database's
That consistency is entirely redundant with the durability property
That consistency cannot be defined precisely enough to be useful
That consistency is the only one of the four that genuinely matters

questions.explanation: A clean separation: three database properties and one application property.

questions.question: Two clients concurrently increment a counter, each doing read, add 1, write, starting from 42. What happens?

options.text: It reaches 43 rather than 44, because one increment is lost
The counter reaches 44 correctly because writes are atomic
The counter reaches 42 because both writes are rejected
One client receives an error and the counter reaches 43

questions.explanation: Read-modify-write without isolation loses one of the two increments.

questions.question: How do the classic database textbooks formalize isolation, and what exactly does the database promise?

options.text: As serializability: each transaction pretends it runs alone
As linearizability, meaning every read sees the latest write
As snapshot isolation, meaning reads come from a consistent snapshot
As atomicity, meaning transactions are indivisible

questions.explanation: Concurrently running transactions shouldn't be able to step on each other's toes.

questions.question: What does the chapter say about serializable isolation in practice, and about Oracle's 'serializable'?

options.text: Rarely used, because of its performance penalty
Serializable isolation is the default in most databases, and Oracle's implementation is genuine
Oracle's serializable level is stronger than the standard requires
Serializable isolation is free in modern databases

questions.explanation: The first of the chapter's several vocabulary traps around isolation-level names.

questions.question: Define durability, and what it means in single-node versus replicated databases.

options.text: That committed data survives a hardware fault or database crash
That the written data survives in memory, making replication irrelevant to durability
That data is written to a cache before commit
That data can be recovered from a nightly backup

questions.explanation: The chapter is clear that perfect durability does not exist: if all your hard disks and all your backups are destroyed at the same time, there's obviously nothing your database can do to save you.

questions.question: The 'Replication and Durability' sidebar traces what durability has meant. What are the stages?

options.text: Archive tape, then disk or SSD, and more recently replication
It has always meant writing to disk, with no historical change
It meant replication first, then disk, then tape
It meant in-memory persistence, then disk

questions.explanation: Three stages, each superseding rather than abolishing the last.

questions.question: Which arguments does the sidebar give on disk versus replication? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: For replication: if data is written to disk and the machine dies, the data isn't lost but it is inaccessible until the machine is repaired or transferred — replicated systems can remain available
For disk: a correlated fault such as a power outage or a bug that crashes on a particular input can knock out all replicas at once, so writing to disk is still relevant even for in-memory databases
For disk: in an asynchronously replicated system, recent writes may be lost when the leader becomes unavailable
Replication to other nodes makes writing to local disk entirely unnecessary

questions.explanation: The two pull in opposite directions, which is why neither is sufficient alone.

questions.question: Which storage-reliability findings does the sidebar cite? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: A study of SSDs found that between 30% and 80% of drives develop at least one bad block during the first four years of operation
Magnetic hard drives have a lower rate of bad sectors but a higher rate of complete failure than SSDs
On SSDs in particular, even fsync isn't guaranteed to work correctly; and an SSD disconnected from power can start losing data within a few weeks, depending on temperature
Solid-state drives never develop bad blocks during their first four years of service

questions.explanation: Disk firmware can have bugs like any other software, subtle interactions between the storage engine and the filesystem can corrupt files after a crash, and if data has been corrupted for some time without being detected you need a historical backup. The conclusion: there is no one technique that can provide absolute guarantees — only risk-reduction techniques, which can and should be used together, and any theoretical guarantee should be taken with a healthy grain of salt.

questions.question: In the email counter example, why is the count stored in a separate field, and what does that oblige you to do?

options.text: Because counting unread messages on every read would be too slow
Because the schema demands the field, so no extra work is involved
Because a count of unread messages cannot be expressed in SQL
Because the counter field is automatically indexed by the database

questions.explanation: Denormalization is what creates the multi-object write that needs a transaction.

questions.question: What does user 2 see in Figure 7-2, and what is the anomaly called?

options.text: The listing shows an unread message while the counter shows zero
User 2 sees the counter but not the message, which is a lost update
User 2 sees neither the counter nor the message, which is write skew
User 2 sees both consistently, so no anomaly has occurred at all

questions.explanation: A footnote defends the example by noting that arguably the counter is an optimization that could be dropped, but a customer account balance in a payment transaction cannot be.

questions.question: Figure 7-2 illustrated isolation. What does Figure 7-3 illustrate?

options.text: Atomicity, so the mailbox and counter cannot go out of sync
Durability, illustrated with exactly the same mailbox example
Consistency, illustrated with a different accounting example
Serializability, illustrated with the counter race from earlier

questions.explanation: Same example, different ACID property — isolation is about other readers, atomicity about partial failure.

questions.question: How do relational databases decide which operations belong to the same transaction, and what problem does a footnote raise?

options.text: By the client's TCP connection, between BEGIN and COMMIT
By session cookie; the footnote notes cookies can be forged
By a per-statement identifier; the footnote notes it is expensive
By a lock table; the footnote notes locks can be lost

questions.explanation: The footnote cites 'The End-to-End Argument for Databases'.

questions.question: Many nonrelational databases offer a multi-put API. Why doesn't that resolve the lack of transactions?

options.text: Because the command may succeed for some keys and fail for others
Because a multi-put is slower than issuing the writes individually
Because a multi-put cannot address more than one key at a time
It does resolve it, because a multi-put is itself a transaction

questions.explanation: A batch API is not an atomicity guarantee.

questions.question: You are writing a 20 KB JSON document. What questions does the chapter ask about single-object writes, and what do storage engines aim to provide?

options.text: Whether the database stores an unparseable fragment of the write
Whether the document is indexed, compressed and replicated; engines aim for durability only
Whether the schema is validated; engines aim for consistency only
Whether the write is fast; engines aim for throughput only

questions.explanation: Single-object atomicity and isolation are essentially universal, unlike multi-object transactions.

questions.question: Which more complex single-object operations does the chapter name, and what do they save you from?

options.text: An increment operation, and a compare-and-set operation
Bulk insert and bulk delete, which save you from locking
Snapshot read and range scan, which save you from phantoms
Commit and rollback, which save you from crashes

questions.explanation: Both remove a read-modify-write cycle from the application.

questions.question: Some vendors call single-object operations 'lightweight transactions'. Why does the chapter refuse the term?

options.text: Because a transaction normally groups multiple objects, not one
Because they are too slow to deserve the name transaction
Because they provide no durability for the value they write
Because they only work on a single node, never across a cluster

questions.explanation: Multiple objects is the defining criterion the term requires.

questions.question: Which cases genuinely need multi-object transactions? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Relational or graph data with references: when a row has a foreign key reference to a row in another table, or when inserting several vertices and edges, you need to ensure these references remain valid or the data becomes nonsensical
Denormalized documents: document databases lack join functionality and so encourage denormalization, so when updating denormalized information you need to update several documents in one go
Databases with secondary indexes: these indexes are different database objects from a transaction point of view, so without isolation it's possible for a record to appear in one index but not another
Single-key counters, which cannot otherwise be incremented safely by concurrent clients

questions.explanation: Single-key counters are exactly what atomic single-object operations handle. The chapter concedes such applications can still be implemented without transactions, but error handling becomes much more complicated without atomicity and the lack of isolation can cause concurrency problems.

questions.question: Why have many distributed datastores abandoned multi-object transactions, and does the chapter accept this as fundamental?

options.text: Because they are hard across partitions and can block availability
Because transactions are mathematically impossible in a distributed system
Because the CAP theorem forbids them
Because no one has attempted to implement them

questions.explanation: Difficult and sometimes unwanted, not impossible.

questions.question: What philosophy do ACID databases follow on aborts, and who rejects it?

options.text: They would rather abandon a transaction than leave it half-finished
ACID databases retry automatically whereas leaderless systems abort
Both families abort in exactly the same circumstances
ACID databases never abort a transaction once it has begun

questions.explanation: Abortability is the ACID stance; best effort is the leaderless one.

questions.question: Which ORM frameworks does the chapter name, and what do they fail to do?

options.text: Rails's ActiveRecord and Django, which raise instead of retrying
Hibernate and Entity Framework; they retry too aggressively
SQLAlchemy and Sequelize; they suppress all errors
They all retry correctly; the chapter praises them

questions.explanation: An abortable transaction that isn't retried wastes the guarantee.

questions.question: Retrying an aborted transaction 'isn't perfect'. Which caveats does the chapter list? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If the transaction actually succeeded but the network failed while the server tried to acknowledge the commit, retrying causes it to be performed twice — unless you have an additional application-level deduplication mechanism in place
If the error is due to overload, retrying will make the problem worse, not better; you can limit the number of retries, use exponential backoff, and handle overload-related errors differently

It is only worth retrying after transient errors such as deadlock, isolation violation, temporary network interruptions and failover — after a permanent error such as a constraint violation a retry would be pointless
If the transaction is retried too quickly, the database will silently apply it twice without reporting an error

questions.explanation: A retry is not silently applied twice — the risk is the opposite, that a side effect outside the database, such as sending an email, happens on every attempt even if the transaction itself is aborted. Five caveats. Retrying is simple and effective but not unconditional.

questions.question: Under what conditions do race conditions come into play?

options.text: Only when transactions read or write the same data concurrently
Whenever two transactions run at the same time, regardless of data
Only when transactions span multiple partitions
Only under serializable isolation

questions.explanation: Data overlap, not mere simultaneity, is the precondition.

questions.question: Why do concurrency bugs resist testing? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They are hard to find by testing, because such bugs are only triggered when you get unlucky with the timing — which may happen very rarely and is usually difficult to reproduce
Concurrency is difficult to reason about, especially in a large application where you don't necessarily know which other pieces of code are accessing the database
Application development is difficult enough with just one user at a time, but having many concurrent users makes it much harder, because any piece of data could unexpectedly change at any time
Test frameworks are unable to run more than one transaction concurrently

questions.explanation: Rarity, irreproducibility and non-local reasoning all work against testing.

questions.question: What is transaction isolation for, and what is the practical problem?

options.text: Transaction isolation, which in theory hides concurrency entirely
Isolation is free and always enabled at the strongest level
Isolation exists only for auditing purposes
Isolation guarantees nothing in any real database

questions.explanation: Some, not all — which is why the chapter enumerates the specific anomalies each level permits.

questions.question: What real-world harm does the chapter attribute to weak isolation bugs, and why does 'use an ACID database for financial data' miss the point? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They have caused substantial loss of money
They have led to investigation by financial auditors
They have caused customer data to be corrupted
Auditors have banned weak isolation levels in regulated financial systems

questions.explanation: No such ban is claimed. The chapter's point about advice is different: telling people to use a 'real' database misses the point, because many popular relational systems considered 'ACID' themselves use weak isolation. The ACID label buys you nothing if the configured isolation level is weak. Rather than blindly relying on tools, we need to develop a good understanding of the kinds of concurrency problems that exist and how to prevent them.

questions.question: State read committed's two guarantees.

options.text: Reads see only committed data; writes overwrite only committed data
Reads come from a consistent snapshot, and writes never block
Transactions execute in a serial order, and aborts are always safe
Reads are repeatable, and phantoms are prevented

questions.explanation: Read committed is the most basic level of transaction isolation. A footnote notes some databases support an even weaker level called read uncommitted, which prevents dirty writes but does not prevent dirty reads.

questions.question: Define a dirty read and the visibility rule read committed enforces.

options.text: Seeing data another transaction has written but not yet committed
A dirty read is reading data that was later deleted; read committed prevents it by locking
A dirty read is reading from a stale replica; read committed routes reads to the leader
A dirty read is reading an aborted write; read committed retries the read

questions.explanation: In Figure 7-4, x starts at 2, user 1 sets x = 3 but has not yet committed, user 2 reads the old value 2, and only after user 1 commits does user 2 see 3.

questions.question: Why is it useful to prevent dirty reads? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Partial updates are visible: if a transaction updates several objects, a dirty read means another transaction may see some of the updates but not others — which is confusing to users and may cause other transactions to take incorrect decisions

Rolled-back data may be observed: if a transaction aborts, any writes it made are rolled back, so without preventing dirty reads a transaction may see data that is later rolled back and was never actually committed — which is mind-bending
Dirty reads cause the stored data on disk to become corrupted
Dirty reads violate durability rather than isolation

questions.explanation: Two reasons: partial visibility and observing writes that never happened.

questions.question: Define a dirty write and how databases prevent it.

options.text: That a later write overwrites an earlier one
A dirty write is writing to an uncommitted read; prevented by snapshots
A dirty write is writing to a stale replica; prevented by quorums
A dirty write is an aborted write; prevented by logging

questions.explanation: Overwriting an uncommitted value is the definition.

questions.question: Trace Figure 7-5, where Alice and Bob simultaneously try to buy the same car.

options.text: The listing goes to one buyer while the invoice goes to another
Both buyers receive invoices and the sale is awarded to neither
The second transaction is rejected, so no mishap occurs even without read committed
Alice gets both the sale and the invoice; the anomaly is a lost update

questions.explanation: Two writes from two transactions interleaving is exactly what dirty-write prevention stops.

questions.question: Read committed prevents dirty writes. Why doesn't that fix the counter race?

options.text: Because the second increment happens after the first commit
Because the counter is a single object, and isolation levels govern multi-object access
Because read committed does not prevent dirty writes after all
It does fix it; the counter race cannot occur under read committed

questions.explanation: The two writes are sequential with respect to commit, so no uncommitted value is overwritten.

questions.question: Which databases does the chapter list as defaulting to read committed?

options.text: Oracle 11g, PostgreSQL, SQL Server 2012 and MemSQL
MySQL, MongoDB and Cassandra, among many others
IBM DB2 and Riak, among a handful of others
Read committed is not the default in any mainstream database

questions.explanation: Very widely deployed, which is why its anomalies matter in practice.

questions.question: Describe the row-level locking protocol that prevents dirty writes.

options.text: Take a row-level lock and hold it until the transaction ends
Locks are held only for the duration of the write statement
Locks are taken by the application explicitly
No locks are taken at all; the writes are ordered by their timestamps

questions.explanation: Held to end of transaction, acquired automatically.

questions.question: One option for preventing dirty reads is a brief read lock. Why does the chapter reject it?

options.text: Because one long write transaction would stall every reader
Because read locks cannot be implemented efficiently on a B-tree
Because acquiring read locks would frequently cause deadlock
Because holding read locks would violate durability guarantees

questions.explanation: Operational coupling across unrelated parts of the application is the objection.

questions.question: How do most databases actually prevent dirty reads?

options.text: Keep both the old committed value and the new uncommitted one
By taking a read lock on every object that is read
By aborting all concurrent readers when a write arrives
By delaying every read until no writes are in flight at all

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that at the time of writing, the only databases that use locks for read committed isolation are IBM DB2 and Microsoft SQL Server in the read_committed_snapshot=off configuration.

questions.question: Alice has $1,000 split across two accounts of $500 each, and a transaction transfers $100 between them. What can Alice observe under read committed?

options.text: She sees one account before the payment and the other after it
She always sees a correct total of $1,000 across the two accounts
She sees $1,100 in total, as though money had been created
She sees an error returned rather than any balance at all

questions.explanation: Alice observes the database in an inconsistent state, even though each value she read was committed at the time she read it.

questions.question: Name the anomaly and say whether read committed is violated.

options.text: Nonrepeatable read, or read skew — acceptable under read committed
It is a dirty read, and read committed isolation is violated by it
It is a lost update, and read committed isolation is violated by it
It is write skew, and read committed isolation is violated by it

questions.explanation: A boxed warning notes the term skew is overloaded: it was previously used for an unbalanced workload with hot spots, whereas here it means a timing anomaly — nothing to do with hot spots.

questions.question: Alice's read skew resolves on reload. Which workloads cannot tolerate it? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Backups: taking a backup requires making a copy of the entire database, which may take hours on a large database, and during that time writes will continue to be made — so you may end up with some parts of the backup containing an older version of the data and other parts containing a newer version. If you then restore from that backup, the inconsistencies such as disappearing money become permanent

Analytic queries and integrity checks: queries that scan over large parts of the database — perhaps for analytics, or a periodic integrity check monitoring for data corruption — are likely to return nonsensical results if they observe parts of the database at different points in time
Single-key point lookups served from an in-memory cache
Atomic increments applied to a single counter column

questions.explanation: Both read large amounts of data over a long window, which is exactly what read skew corrupts.

questions.question: Define snapshot isolation.

options.text: Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot of the database
Each transaction reads the latest committed value at the time of each statement
Each transaction holds read locks for its duration
Each transaction executes serially on one thread

questions.explanation: It is a boon for long-running, read-only queries such as backups and analytics, because the data does not change under the query. It is supported by PostgreSQL, MySQL with the InnoDB storage engine, Oracle and SQL Server, among others.

questions.question: What locking does snapshot isolation use, and what is the resulting mantra?

options.text: Write locks prevent dirty writes, but readers never block writers
It uses read locks and write locks; readers block writers and vice versa
It uses no locks at all; conflicts are detected at commit
It uses table-level locks only

questions.explanation: This mantra is precisely what two-phase locking inverts.

questions.question: Why must the database keep several versions of an object, and what is the technique called?

options.text: Because in-progress transactions may need several committed versions
Because writes are append-only; the technique is log-structured storage
Because replicas diverge; the technique is version vectors
Because indexes need old values; the technique is copy-on-write

questions.explanation: Multiple in-flight snapshot points is what forces multiple versions.

questions.question: How do read committed and snapshot isolation differ in an MVCC engine?

options.text: Two versions suffice for read committed; snapshots need many more
Read committed needs four versions; snapshot isolation needs two
Read committed uses one snapshot per transaction; snapshot isolation uses one per query
They are implemented identically

questions.explanation: Per-query versus per-transaction snapshot is the whole distinction.

questions.question: How are transaction IDs assigned in the PostgreSQL implementation?

options.text: An always-increasing transaction ID that tags everything it writes
Transaction IDs are random UUIDs, so overflow can never occur
Transaction IDs are wall-clock timestamps taken from the node
Transaction IDs are reused as soon as the transaction commits

questions.explanation: Always-increasing is the property the visibility rules depend on.

questions.question: Describe the two per-row fields in the MVCC table, and what happens on a delete.

options.text: created_by holds the inserting transaction ID; deleted_by the deleting one
Each row has a version number and a checksum; deletes remove the row immediately
Each row has a lock field and a timestamp; deletes set the timestamp to zero
Each row has only a created_by field; deletes append a tombstone row

questions.explanation: Marking rather than removing is what lets older snapshots still see the row.

questions.question: How is an update represented internally, and what does the accounts table contain after transaction 13 deducts $100 from account 2?

options.text: As a delete plus a create, leaving two rows for the account
The single row's balance field is overwritten in place from $500 to $400
A new table is created holding the new value
The old row is deleted immediately and only the new row remains

questions.explanation: Delete-plus-create is what makes an update a new version rather than a mutation.

questions.question: Which visibility rules let a transaction observe a consistent snapshot? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: At the start of each transaction, the database makes a list of all the other transactions that are in progress at that time; any writes those transactions have made are ignored, even if the transactions subsequently commit
Any writes made by aborted transactions are ignored
Writes made by transactions with an earlier transaction ID are ignored if they committed after this transaction started
All other writes are visible to the application's queries — and these rules apply to both creation and deletion of objects

questions.explanation: The rule runs the other way: writes made by transactions with a later transaction ID are ignored, regardless of whether those transactions have committed. Four rules, applying symmetrically to creates and deletes.

questions.question: Why does transaction 12 see $500 for account 2 in Figure 7-7, and what is the two-condition restatement of the rules?

options.text: Because transaction 12 cannot see transaction 13's deletion
Because transaction 12 holds a read lock on the row
Because transaction 13 aborted
Because transaction 12 started after transaction 13 committed

questions.explanation: A long-running transaction may continue using a snapshot for a long time, continuing to read values that other transactions have since overwritten or deleted. By never updating values in place but instead creating a new version every time a value is changed, the database can provide a consistent snapshot at only a small overhead.

questions.question: How can indexes work in a multi-version database?

options.text: Point the index at all versions and filter by visibility on read
Indexes must be rebuilt on every write
Indexes point only to the newest version, so old versions are unindexed
Multi-version databases cannot have indexes

questions.explanation: Point at all versions and filter on read, garbage-collecting index entries alongside rows.

questions.question: Describe the append-only / copy-on-write B-tree approach and which systems use it.

options.text: Append-only or copy-on-write B-trees, as in CouchDB, Datomic and LMDB
PostgreSQL, MySQL and Oracle use it; it requires no garbage collection
It overwrites pages in place but keeps a version stamp per page
It copies the entire tree on every write

questions.explanation: Immutability gives snapshots for free, at the cost of compaction.

questions.question: What does each vendor call snapshot isolation, and why do the names diverge?

options.text: Oracle calls it serializable; PostgreSQL and MySQL call it repeatable read
All vendors call it snapshot isolation; the standard defines it explicitly
Oracle calls it repeatable read and PostgreSQL calls it serializable
The SQL standard defines snapshot isolation, and vendors deviate arbitrarily

questions.explanation: A gap in a 1975-derived standard is what produced the naming chaos.

questions.question: Give the chapter's indictment of the SQL standard's isolation levels.

options.text: That its definition of isolation levels is ambiguous and imprecise
The standard is precise and implementations are consistent
The standard has no definition of isolation levels at all
The standard is precise but too strict for implementers

questions.explanation: 'Nobody really knows what repeatable read means' is the closing verdict.

questions.question: Define the lost update problem and the verb the chapter uses.

options.text: Two concurrent read-modify-write cycles, where one write is lost
It occurs when a write is rolled back on commit; the verb is discard
It occurs when a replica misses a write; the verb is drop
It occurs when two transactions read the same value; the verb is stale

questions.explanation: Read committed and snapshot isolation were primarily about what a read-only transaction can see in the presence of concurrent writes; this section turns to two transactions writing concurrently.

questions.question: Which read-modify-write scenarios does the chapter give? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Incrementing a counter or updating an account balance — requires reading the current value, calculating the new value, and writing back the updated value
Making a local change to a complex value, for example adding an element to a list within a JSON document — requires parsing the document, making the change, and writing back the modified document
Two users editing a wiki page at the same time, where each user saves their changes by sending the entire page contents to the server, overwriting whatever is currently in the database
Reading a single row by its primary key with no subsequent write to it

questions.explanation: Three scenarios, all sharing the read-modify-write shape.

questions.question: Which solution does the chapter call the best, and which systems does it name?

options.text: Atomic write operations, such as an increment inside the database
Explicit application-level locking, which is always the safest route
Last write wins, which is the simplest thing that can work
Compare-and-set, which is universally supported by databases

questions.explanation: Not all writes can easily be expressed as atomic operations — for example updates to a wiki page involve arbitrary text editing. A footnote notes it is possible, albeit fairly complicated, to express the editing of a text document as a stream of atomic mutations.

questions.question: How are atomic operations implemented?

options.text: An exclusive lock taken when the row is read — SELECT FOR UPDATE
By optimistic retry, with no locking of the row at all
By relying on snapshot isolation alone to serialize them
By running the update inside a two-phase commit protocol

questions.explanation: Cursor stability is the name for the read-with-exclusive-lock approach.

questions.question: What does the chapter say ORM frameworks do to lost-update safety?

options.text: They make unsafe read-modify-write cycles easy to write by accident
They automatically convert read-modify-write cycles into atomic operations
They prevent every kind of lost update by default configuration
They have no bearing at all on whether lost updates occur

questions.explanation: The convenience of the abstraction hides the unsafe pattern.

questions.question: In the multiplayer game example, why is an atomic operation insufficient and what does the SQL do?

options.text: Because the move must also satisfy the rules of the game
Because atomic operations cannot touch more than one row; FOR UPDATE creates a snapshot
Because the game is distributed; FOR UPDATE replicates the lock
An atomic operation is sufficient; FOR UPDATE is redundant

questions.explanation: Application logic that can't be pushed into the database is what forces explicit locking. The catch: to get it right you need to carefully think about your application logic, and it's easy to forget to add a necessary lock somewhere.

questions.question: Contrast automatic lost update detection with locks and atomic operations.

options.text: Let the writes proceed and abort the transaction that lost the race
Detection is slower than locking in every workload measured
Detection requires transactions to be executed serially
Detection and locking are really the same mechanism renamed

questions.explanation: Optimistic parallel execution plus abort-on-detect, riding on MVCC bookkeeping.

questions.question: Which isolation levels automatically detect lost updates? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: PostgreSQL's repeatable read
Oracle's serializable
SQL Server's snapshot isolation level
MySQL/InnoDB's repeatable read

questions.explanation: MySQL/InnoDB's repeatable read does not detect lost updates. Some authors argue that a database must prevent lost updates in order to qualify as providing snapshot isolation, so MySQL does not provide snapshot isolation under this definition.

questions.question: Why does the chapter call lost update detection 'a great feature'?

options.text: Because it needs no special database features to be used correctly
Because it is measurably faster than taking explicit locks
Because it continues to work across multiple replicas
Because it never needs to abort a transaction to succeed

questions.explanation: Safety that does not depend on the developer remembering something.

questions.question: Describe compare-and-set for the wiki page, and when it isn't safe.

options.text: An atomic compare-and-set, updating only if the value is unchanged
Compare-and-set is always safe in every database
Compare-and-set requires an exclusive lock, making it equivalent to FOR UPDATE
Compare-and-set cannot be expressed in SQL

questions.explanation: A stale-snapshot WHERE clause silently defeats the mechanism.

questions.question: Why don't lock and compare-and-set techniques transfer to multi-leader or leaderless replication, and what is used instead?

options.text: Because both assume a single up-to-date copy of the data
Because replication is synchronous; quorums are used instead
Because locks are too slow; timestamps are used instead
They do transfer without modification

questions.explanation: No single up-to-date copy means nothing to lock against.

questions.question: Which kind of operation works well in a replicated context, and what default does the chapter warn against?

options.text: Commutative atomic operations, which can be applied in any order
Non-commutative operations work best; LWW is safe
Only read-only operations work; LWW is recommended
Commutative operations are unsafe; locks are recommended

questions.explanation: Order-independence is what makes merging possible without coordination.

questions.question: State the hospital on-call invariant and when a doctor may give up a shift.

options.text: That at least one doctor must always remain on call
Exactly two doctors must be on call at all times, with no exceptions
Doctors may never give up shifts
At least three doctors must be on call, and any may leave

questions.explanation: 'At least one' is the invariant the write skew violates.

questions.question: Trace Figure 7-8 where Alice and Bob both click 'go off call' simultaneously under snapshot isolation.

options.text: Both transactions see two doctors on call, so both go off call
One check returns 2 and the other returns 1, so only Alice succeeds
Both checks return 1, so neither proceeds
Snapshot isolation prevents this; the second transaction aborts

questions.explanation: Figure 7-8's caption: example of write skew causing an application bug.

questions.question: Why is write skew neither a dirty write nor a lost update?

options.text: Because the two transactions update two different rows
Because no writes occurred in either of the two transactions
Because both of the transactions updated the very same object
Because the two transactions happened to be serialized anyway

questions.explanation: Different objects written, shared premise read — that is the shape of write skew.

questions.question: State the general definition of write skew, and how the other anomalies fall out of it.

options.text: Two transactions read the same objects, then update different ones
Write skew is a special case of the lost update problem
Write skew and lost update describe unrelated phenomena
Write skew is a special case of the dirty read problem

questions.explanation: The general case first, with the same-object cases as specializations.

questions.question: Which of these prevent write skew automatically: PostgreSQL's repeatable read, MySQL/InnoDB's repeatable read, Oracle's serializable, SQL Server's snapshot isolation?

options.text: None of them — write skew is not automatically detected
All four of the listed mechanisms prevent it automatically
Only Oracle's serializable isolation level prevents it
Only PostgreSQL's repeatable read level prevents it

questions.explanation: Note the contrast with lost updates: three of those four do detect lost updates, but none detects write skew.

questions.question: Could a database constraint enforce the on-call rule?

options.text: Not easily, since most constraints involve only a single object
Yes, a uniqueness constraint on the shift is sufficient
Yes, a foreign key constraint on the doctor is sufficient
No, and the chapter offers no workaround of any kind

questions.explanation: Multi-object constraints are the gap. If you can't use a serializable isolation level, the second-best option is probably to explicitly lock the rows the transaction depends on with SELECT FOR UPDATE.

questions.question: In the meeting room booking example, what is being enforced and why does it fail?

options.text: That there cannot be two bookings for one room at one time
It enforces room capacity, and fails because of lost updates
It enforces booking duration, and fails because of dirty reads
It succeeds under snapshot isolation

questions.explanation: A footnote notes that PostgreSQL's range types make it possible to define a constraint here elegantly, but they are not widely supported in other databases.

questions.question: The multiplayer game appeared earlier under lost updates. What different problem does it illustrate here?

options.text: It stops two players moving one figure, not two figures to one square
It illustrates dirty reads rather than write skew at all
It illustrates phantoms arising in read-only queries
It illustrates deadlock between two transactions under 2PL

questions.explanation: Different objects, same shared rule — the write skew signature.

questions.question: Describe the username write skew and why this case is easier than the others.

options.text: Two users concurrently claiming the same unique username
It is harder because usernames are not indexable
It requires materializing conflicts
It requires serializable isolation with no simpler option

questions.explanation: The invariant happens to be exactly a single-object uniqueness rule, which databases do support.

questions.question: Describe the double-spending implementation and how write skew breaks it.

options.text: Two concurrent spends that each pass the balance check
The balance is overwritten by a lost update
A dirty read shows a stale balance
The implementation is safe under snapshot isolation

questions.explanation: Each transaction's sum is computed on a snapshot that excludes the other's insert.

questions.question: For which write-skew examples does the chapter say a database constraint is a workable fix? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Claiming a username — a unique constraint is a simple solution here
The multiplayer game — sometimes, depending on the kind of rule, a unique constraint may work
The doctor on call — no, it would need a constraint involving multiple objects
The meeting room booking — yes, a simple uniqueness constraint on room_id is sufficient

questions.explanation: A uniqueness constraint on room_id would forbid a room ever being booked twice. The chapter says you once again need serializable isolation, though PostgreSQL range types can help. All four statements are accurate: two are workable (one fully, one conditionally) and two are not.

questions.question: All the write-skew examples follow the same pattern. What are the three steps?

options.text: A SELECT that checks a precondition, then a write that depends on it
Lock the rows, write the change, then commit the transaction
Begin the transaction, write, then roll the change back
Read the value, merge it locally, then retry the write

questions.explanation: The steps may occur in a different order — for example you could first make the write, then the SELECT query, and finally decide whether to abort or commit.

questions.question: Why does the write in step 3 invalidate the check in step 1? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The effect of the write changes the precondition of the decision of step 2 — if you were to repeat the SELECT query from step 1 after committing the write, you would get a different result, because the write changed the set of rows matching the search condition
There is now one fewer doctor on call, or the meeting room is now booked for that time
The position on the board is now taken by the figure that was moved, or the username is now taken
A different transaction ID is now recorded against the row that was written

questions.explanation: The transaction ID is bookkeeping, not the precondition. The fourth concrete effect the chapter lists is that there is now less money in the account. Five restatements of the same structural fact across the five examples.

questions.question: The doctors example can be made safe with SELECT FOR UPDATE. Why can't the other four?

options.text: Because the modified row was one of the rows the check returned
Because the other examples each involve more than one table
Because FOR UPDATE is not supported for those query shapes
Because the other examples turn out to be read-only anyway

questions.explanation: You cannot lock rows that don't exist yet — which is exactly the phantom problem.

questions.question: Define a phantom, and what snapshot isolation does about it.

options.text: A phantom — a write that changes another query's result set
A phantom is an aborted write; snapshot isolation removes it entirely
A phantom is a stale read; snapshot isolation prevents it in all transactions
A phantom is a deadlock; snapshot isolation detects it

questions.explanation: Read-only queries are safe; read-write ones are not.

questions.question: Describe the materializing conflicts technique for the meeting room case.

options.text: Introduce a lock object artificially, as rows to be locked
It creates a trigger that rejects overlapping bookings
It switches to serial execution for booking transactions only
It hashes the room and time into a single key

questions.explanation: Turning a non-existent row into an existing lockable one is the trick.

questions.question: What is the chapter's recommendation about materializing conflicts?

options.text: It is error-prone, and lets concurrency control leak into the data model
It is the recommended default approach for most applications
It is always preferable to true serializable isolation
It should be used whenever phantoms are theoretically possible

questions.explanation: Last resort, not first choice.

questions.question: The chapter summarizes why weak isolation is unsatisfying. Which points does it make? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Isolation levels are hard to understand and inconsistently implemented in different databases — for example the meaning of 'repeatable read' varies significantly

If you look at your application code it's difficult to tell whether it is safe to run at a particular isolation level, especially in a large application where you might not be aware of all the things that may be happening concurrently

There are no good tools to help us detect race conditions: static analysis tools may help, but they have not yet found their way into practical use, and testing for concurrency issues is hard because they are usually nondeterministic
The problem is entirely new, having appeared only with distributed databases

questions.explanation: The problem is not new: it has been like this since the 1970s, when weak isolation levels were first introduced — and researchers' answer has always been simple: use serializable isolation.

questions.question: What does serializable isolation guarantee, and what is the strong claim?

options.text: That the result is the same as if transactions had run one at a time
It guarantees only that every read comes from a consistent snapshot
It guarantees that no transaction will ever need to be aborted
It guarantees that all writes are durable once committed

questions.explanation: All possible race conditions is an unusually strong claim, which raises the obvious question of why isn't everyone using it — answered by looking at the options for implementing serializability and how they perform.

questions.question: Name the three techniques most databases providing serializability use today.

options.text: Serial execution, two-phase locking, and optimistic concurrency control
Quorum reads, version vectors and conflict-free replicated datatypes
Snapshot isolation, read committed and read uncommitted levels
Two-phase commit, distributed consensus and leader election

questions.explanation: The chapter considers these mostly in the context of single-node databases; Chapter 9 examines whether they can be generalized to transactions that involve multiple nodes in a distributed system.

questions.question: Describe actual serial execution and why its isolation is serializable by definition.

options.text: Remove concurrency entirely by running one transaction at a time
It runs transactions in parallel but commits them in order
It uses one thread per transaction with locking
It batches transactions and applies them atomically

questions.explanation: No concurrency means nothing to reconcile.

questions.question: When did database designers decide a single-threaded execution loop was feasible?

options.text: Around 2007
In 1975, with System R
In 1999, with the SQL/PSM standard
In 2015, with the rise of in-memory databases

questions.explanation: A reversal of 30 years of accepted wisdom.

questions.question: Which developments made single-threaded execution viable? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: RAM became cheap enough that for many use cases it is now feasible to keep the entire active dataset in memory, so when all data a transaction needs is in memory, transactions can execute much faster than if they have to wait for data to be loaded from disk
Database designers realized that OLTP transactions are usually short and only make a small number of reads and writes
Long-running analytic queries are typically read-only, so they can be run on a consistent snapshot using snapshot isolation, outside of the serial execution loop
CPU clock speeds increased dramatically after 2007, making threads unnecessary

questions.explanation: Clock speeds notably did not increase — that is the trend that made multi-core matter.

questions.question: Which systems execute transactions serially, and what limits the approach?

options.text: VoltDB/H-Store, Redis and Datomic
PostgreSQL and MySQL, limited by disk bandwidth
Cassandra and Riak, limited by network latency
Oracle and SQL Server, limited by memory

questions.explanation: One core is the hard ceiling, which is why partitioning matters here.

questions.question: What did database designers originally intend a transaction to encompass?

options.text: A whole flow of user activity, such as an entire airline booking
A single row update, exactly as in a modern web application
A batch of writes applied together overnight
One segment of the database's replication log

questions.explanation: The ambition failed because humans are very slow to make up their minds and respond: to support it, databases would need to support a potentially huge number of concurrent transactions, most of them idle, and most databases cannot do that efficiently.

questions.question: What boundary replaced the human-scale transaction on the web?

options.text: By never waiting interactively for a user inside a transaction
A transaction spans the user's entire browsing session
A transaction spans a whole day of a user's activity
A transaction spans one TCP connection, however many requests

questions.explanation: One request, one transaction — humans removed from the critical section.

questions.question: Why does the interactive client/server style make serial execution unusable?

options.text: Because so much of the time is spent on network round-trips
Because interactive transactions cannot be aborted
Because interactive transactions cannot be logged
Because interactive transactions violate isolation

questions.explanation: Network round-trips would idle the single thread.

questions.question: What do single-threaded systems require instead of interactive transactions?

options.text: The whole transaction must be submitted ahead of time as a stored procedure
They require the client to batch all statements in one request without stored procedures
They require the client to hold a lock for the duration
They require the transaction to be split across threads

questions.explanation: Figure 7-9 illustrates the contrast using the doctors-going-off-call example from Figure 7-8.

questions.question: Why do stored procedures have a bad reputation? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Each database vendor has its own language for stored procedures — Oracle has PL/SQL, SQL Server has T-SQL, PostgreSQL has PL/pgSQL — and these languages haven't kept up with developments in general-purpose programming languages, so they look quite ugly and archaic and lack the ecosystem of libraries you find in most programming languages

Code running in a database is difficult to manage: it is harder to debug, more awkward to keep in version control and deploy, trickier to test, and difficult to integrate with a metrics collection system for monitoring

A database is often much more performance-sensitive than an application server, because a single database instance is often shared by many application servers — so a badly written stored procedure can cause much more trouble than equivalent badly written code in an application server
Stored procedures are not part of any published database standard

questions.explanation: They have been part of the SQL standard, SQL/PSM, since 1999.

questions.question: Which languages do modern stored-procedure systems use?

options.text: VoltDB uses Java or Groovy, Datomic Java or Clojure, Redis Lua
All three of them use PL/SQL for stored procedures
VoltDB uses Lua, Datomic uses Groovy, and Redis uses Java
All three of them use Microsoft's T-SQL dialect

questions.explanation: General-purpose languages plus in-memory data are what made the single thread viable.

questions.question: What else does VoltDB use stored procedures for, and what does that require?

options.text: Run the same stored procedure on every replica instead of shipping writes
For indexing, which requires that the procedures be idempotent
For partitioning, which requires that the procedures be commutative
For backups, which requires no special property of the procedures

questions.explanation: Determinism is what lets the procedure itself be the replication log entry.

questions.question: How does partitioning let serial execution scale, and what cross-partition throughput does VoltDB report?

options.text: Partition so each transaction touches only one partition
Partitioning has no effect; throughput is always one core
Cross-partition writes reach 100,000 per second
Cross-partition writes scale linearly with machines

questions.explanation: Whether transactions can be single-partition depends on the data: simple key-value data can often be partitioned very easily, but data with multiple secondary indexes is likely to require a lot of cross-partition coordination.

questions.question: Within which constraints is serial execution viable? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Every transaction must be small and fast, because it takes only one slow transaction to stall all transaction processing

It is limited to use cases where the active dataset can fit in memory; rarely accessed data could potentially be moved to disk, but if it needed to be accessed in a single-threaded transaction the system would get very slow
Write throughput must be low enough to be handled on a single CPU core, or else transactions need to be partitioned without requiring cross-partition coordination
Cross-partition transactions are impossible, so the dataset has to partition perfectly along transaction boundaries

questions.explanation: They are possible — there is simply a hard limit to how much they can be used, because they must be coordinated across partition threads. A footnote notes that if a transaction needs to access data that's not in memory, the best solution may be to abort the transaction, asynchronously fetch the data into memory while continuing to process other transactions, and then restart the transaction — an approach known as anti-caching.

questions.question: For how long was two-phase locking the only widely used serializability algorithm?

options.text: Around 30 years
Around 10 years
Around 5 years
It has never been widely used

questions.explanation: A boxed warning notes that while two-phase locking (2PL) sounds very similar to two-phase commit (2PC), they are completely different things — 2PC is discussed in Chapter 9.

questions.question: State the two blocking rules that make 2PL's lock requirements much stronger than dirty-write prevention.

options.text: Concurrent readers are allowed until someone wants to write
Readers never block writers and writers never block readers
Only writers block writers; readers are always free
Locks are held only for the duration of each statement

questions.explanation: In 2PL writers don't just block other writers; they also block readers and vice versa — the exact inverse of snapshot isolation's mantra, which captures the key difference between them. Because 2PL provides serializability, it protects against all the race conditions discussed earlier, including lost updates and write skew.

questions.question: Which databases use 2PL, and for which isolation level?

options.text: Serializable in MySQL InnoDB and SQL Server; repeatable read in DB2
The read committed isolation level in PostgreSQL and Oracle
The snapshot isolation level in SQL Server, and nowhere else
Two-phase locking is not used by any mainstream database today

questions.explanation: DB2's 'repeatable read' means serializability, which is why it is implemented with 2PL.

questions.question: Describe 2PL's two lock modes and acquisition rules.

options.text: Shared mode for reads, exclusive mode for writes
There is only one mode, exclusive, used for both reads and writes
There are three modes: read, write and intent
Shared locks block each other; exclusive locks do not

questions.explanation: If a transaction first reads and then writes an object it may upgrade its shared lock to an exclusive lock, which behaves the same as getting an exclusive lock directly. Once a transaction has acquired the lock it must continue to hold the lock until the end of the transaction — hence 'two-phase': the first phase, while the transaction is executing, is when the locks are acquired, and the second phase, at the end of the transaction, is when all the locks are released.

questions.question: Define deadlock in the 2PL context, and say who resolves it.

options.text: Because two transactions can each wait on the other's lock — deadlock
The application detects the deadlock and the database retries the loser
Deadlock cannot arise under two-phase locking by construction
Deadlocks resolve themselves after a timeout without any abort

questions.explanation: Database detects and aborts; application retries.

questions.question: State 2PL's big downside and its causes, in the chapter's order of importance.

options.text: Performance — throughput and response times are much worse
Durability: writes may be lost on deadlock abort
Correctness: 2PL does not actually provide serializability
Complexity: 2PL is hard to implement, but performance is fine

questions.explanation: Reduced concurrency, not lock bookkeeping, is the dominant cost.

questions.question: Why is there no bound on how long a transaction may wait under 2PL?

options.text: Because transaction duration is unbounded when humans are involved
Because a transaction has a hard 30-second timeout that is often exceeded
Because detecting a deadlock takes longer than the transaction itself
There is a bound on duration, namely the configured lock timeout

questions.explanation: Unbounded transaction duration plus queueing gives unbounded waits.

questions.question: Describe 2PL's latency behaviour and the operational risk.

options.text: Unstable latencies, very slow at high percentiles under contention
Latencies are stable, but uniformly higher than under weak isolation
Latencies are entirely unaffected by contention in the workload
Latencies suffer at the median but not at the higher percentiles

questions.explanation: Deadlocks can also happen with lock-based read committed isolation, but they occur much more frequently under 2PL serializable isolation — and when a transaction is aborted due to deadlock and retried, it needs to do its work all over again, which can mean significant wasted effort if deadlocks are frequent.

questions.question: What must a serializable database prevent that object locks cannot, and what is the mechanism?

options.text: Phantoms — one transaction changing another's search results
Deadlocks, which are prevented by maintaining a wait-for graph
Lost updates, which are prevented by compare-and-set operations
Dirty reads, which are prevented by taking shared read locks

questions.explanation: For the meeting room example, if one transaction has searched for bookings for a room in a time window, another is not allowed to concurrently insert or update another booking for the same room and time range — but it is okay to concurrently insert bookings for other rooms, or for the same room at a different time.

questions.question: What is 'the key idea' about predicate locks?

options.text: That it covers objects which do not yet exist in the database
That a predicate lock is cheaper to acquire than an object lock
That two predicate locks can never conflict with one another
That a predicate lock applies only to rows that already exist

questions.explanation: Locking the future is what closes the phantom hole.

questions.question: Why are predicate locks replaced in practice, and by what?

options.text: Because checking many predicate locks becomes too time-consuming
They are replaced by timestamps, which are cheaper
They are replaced by table locks in all cases
They are not replaced at all; predicate locks are used in every 2PL database

questions.explanation: Over-approximating the predicate is conservative and therefore safe.

questions.question: Where is the range lock attached, and what is the fallback?

options.text: An index on room_id, with a shared lock on the matching index entry
The lock is attached to the row itself; the fallback is a predicate lock
The lock is attached to the transaction; the fallback is abort
The lock is attached to the connection; the fallback is a timeout

questions.explanation: Index-range locks are not as precise as predicate locks — they lock a bigger range of objects than is strictly necessary — but since they have much lower overheads, they are a good compromise.

questions.question: What dilemma does the chapter say it has painted, and what question does it ask?

options.text: That serializable implementations perform or scale badly
That all three approaches perform equally; the question is which to standardize
That weak isolation is always sufficient; the question is why serializability exists
That serializability is unattainable, so the only question is which weak level to use

questions.explanation: Which SSI is offered as an answer to.

questions.question: What does serializable snapshot isolation offer, and whose work is it?

options.text: Full serializability at only a small penalty over snapshot isolation
It provides snapshot isolation only; first described in 1975 by System R
It provides serializability with a large penalty; described by Cahill in 1998
It provides read committed only; described by Härder and Reuter

questions.explanation: It is used in single-node databases — the serializable isolation level in PostgreSQL since version 9.1 — and in distributed databases, with FoundationDB using a similar algorithm. Because SSI is so young compared to other concurrency control mechanisms, it is still proving its performance in practice, but it has the possibility of being fast enough to become the new default in the future.

questions.question: In what sense is 2PL pessimistic, and serial execution 'pessimistic to the extreme'?

options.text: Pessimistic — wait until it is safe before proceeding
2PL is optimistic and serial execution is pessimistic
Both are optimistic mechanisms, whereas SSI alone is pessimistic
Neither of them is pessimistic; both let transactions proceed and check later

questions.explanation: Serial execution is a whole-database lock, made tolerable by short critical sections.

questions.question: Define optimistic concurrency control and the rule about committing.

options.text: Let transactions proceed and check for violations only at commit
Transactions block on every potential conflict and retry on timeout
Transactions acquire all locks up front and never abort
Transactions run serially but commit optimistically

questions.explanation: Proceed and verify, rather than wait and proceed.

questions.question: Under what conditions does optimistic concurrency control perform badly, and why?

options.text: It performs badly under high contention, as many transactions abort
It performs badly only when contention is unusually low
It performs badly only in the presence of long read-only queries
It outperforms pessimistic control under all conditions

questions.explanation: Optimistic concurrency control is an old idea, and its advantages and disadvantages have been debated for a long time. The retry feedback loop is the specific failure mode.

questions.question: Under what conditions does optimistic control win, and what reduces contention?

options.text: With spare capacity and low contention, optimistic tends to win
Under high contention, which is reduced by taking locks instead
Under low spare capacity, which is reduced by serial execution
Under all conditions, which is reduced by partitioning the data

questions.explanation: The caveat on commutativity — not reading the counter in the same transaction — matters.

questions.question: What is SSI built on, and what does it add?

options.text: It is built on snapshot isolation, reading from a consistent snapshot
It is built on two-phase locking and adds snapshots on top
It is built on serial execution and adds partitioning on top
It is built on read committed and adds predicate locks on top

questions.explanation: Snapshot reads plus conflict detection at commit.

questions.question: Restate the write skew pattern in terms of a 'premise'.

options.text: A read, a decision based on it, and a write that acts on the decision
A transaction writes first and then reads, invalidating its own write
A transaction reads twice and gets different results
A transaction holds a lock on data it never reads

questions.explanation: Naming the read result a premise is what lets the database reason about it mechanically.

questions.question: Why must the database be conservative about premises?

options.text: Because it cannot know how the application uses a query's result
Because the application always declares its premises explicitly
Because premises are stored in the transaction log
Because the database can infer application logic from the query

questions.explanation: Opacity of application logic is what forces conservatism.

questions.question: Which two cases must the database consider, and what is the timing of each?

options.text: Stale MVCC reads, and writes that affect a transaction's prior reads
Detecting dirty reads and dirty writes, both before the commit
Detecting deadlocks and phantoms, both at commit time
Detecting lost updates and read skew, both after the commit

questions.explanation: The two cases are distinguished by whether the conflicting write precedes or follows the read.

questions.question: Trace Figure 7-10 with transactions 42 and 43.

options.text: Because MVCC readers deliberately ignore uncommitted writes
Transaction 43 sees on_call = false and commits successfully
Transaction 42 aborts and 43 commits with no conflict
Both transactions abort immediately on the stale read

questions.explanation: Track the ignored writes, then check them at commit.

questions.question: Why doesn't SSI abort transaction 43 the moment the stale read is detected? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: If transaction 43 was a read-only transaction, it wouldn't need to be aborted, because there is no risk of write skew
At the time when transaction 43 makes its read, the database doesn't yet know whether that transaction is going to later perform a write
Transaction 42 may yet abort or may still be uncommitted at the time when transaction 43 is committed, so the read may turn out not to have been stale after all
Aborting the transaction early would violate the durability guarantee

questions.explanation: By avoiding unnecessary aborts, SSI preserves snapshot isolation's support for long-running reads from a consistent snapshot.

questions.question: For the second case, what mechanism does SSI borrow from 2PL and how does it differ?

options.text: Index-range locks that record reads without blocking other transactions
Predicate locks, which do block other transactions from writing
Table-level locks, held until the next garbage collection pass
Row locks, held only for the duration of the single statement

questions.explanation: Same bookkeeping structure, no blocking behaviour.

questions.question: What must a writing transaction do, and how does the chapter describe the difference from a write lock?

options.text: Look in the indexes for transactions that recently read that data
It must block until all readers have committed, exactly like a write lock
It must abort all readers immediately
It need do nothing; readers check at their own commit time

questions.explanation: A tripwire rather than a barrier — notify, don't block.

questions.question: In Figure 7-11 both transactions notify each other. Which commits and why?

options.text: Each notifies the other; the first to commit succeeds, the second aborts
Both commit, since neither had committed when the notifications arrived
Both abort, since each of them notified the other of a stale read
Transaction 43 commits and transaction 42 is the one that aborts

questions.explanation: Commit ordering decides the winner: whoever commits first wins.

questions.question: What trade-off does the chapter name in SSI's engineering, and what theory does PostgreSQL exploit?

options.text: The granularity at which reads and writes are tracked
The choice between optimistic and pessimistic locking; PostgreSQL uses 2PL theory
The number of snapshot versions retained; PostgreSQL uses garbage collection theory
The abort timeout; PostgreSQL uses queueing theory

questions.explanation: Precision versus overhead, with a provability escape hatch.

questions.question: Compare SSI with 2PL and with serial execution, and state the constraint the abort rate imposes.

options.text: That a transaction never blocks waiting for another's locks
SSI blocks like 2PL and is limited to one core like serial execution
SSI blocks readers but not writers, and scales to one machine
SSI has no abort rate constraint

questions.explanation: Non-blocking like snapshot isolation, distributable unlike serial execution, but abort-rate sensitive. Long-running read-only transactions may be able to proceed without aborting.

questions.question: Give the summary's definition of what transactions are for.

options.text: An abstraction hiding concurrency problems and certain faults
Transactions are a locking mechanism for protecting shared data
Transactions are a durability guarantee for writes
Transactions are a performance optimization for batched writes

questions.explanation: Errors collapsed into one retryable outcome is the abstraction's payoff.

questions.question: Which applications can manage without transactions, and what do transactions buy the rest?

options.text: Not every application is susceptible to every one of those problems
Only financial applications have any real need for transactions
All applications need transactions to exactly the same degree
Only applications distributed across machines need transactions

questions.explanation: Access-pattern complexity, not data sensitivity, is the criterion.

questions.question: Which error scenarios does the summary name for life without transactions, and what concrete inconsistency?

options.text: Crashes, network interruptions, power outages, disk full, and concurrency
Only concurrency problems arise; faults are handled by replication
Only hardware faults arise; concurrency is handled by the application
No inconsistency arises without them; transactions are purely a convenience

questions.explanation: Denormalized data drifting from its source is the concrete example given.
